title: Federated Graph-Level Clustering with Dual Knowledge Separation
one_liner: Split each graph into two pieces — keep the changeable patterns local, send only the stable cluster patterns to the server for smarter aggregation.
lead: When machines learn from thousands of small graphs spread across different computers (federated learning), they face a puzzle: which patterns are unique to each location, and which patterns define the clusters everyone shares? This paper separates the two before aggregating, preventing the server from mixing incompatible ideas together.

paras: A typical federated setup: you have thousands of small graphs (social networks, biological structures, flow diagrams) scattered across hospitals, factories, or banks. Each holds privacy-sensitive data. You want to group similar graphs into clusters without copying the raw data to a central server.

The naive attempt: each machine trains a clustering model locally, then sends it to the server, which averages all the models together. The problem: your local graph patterns are not the same as the cluster patterns everyone shares. When you average them blindly, the server mixes together things that contradict — a pattern that is useful for your local privacy-sensitive subgraph becomes noise for graphs in cluster 7, pulling the shared pattern in the wrong direction. The clustering fails; nobody gets a clean answer.

callout.html: When each machine sends its whole learned pattern to the server without saying which parts are local quirks and which parts define the shared cluster, the server cannot separate them and averages incompatible patterns together.

panels.title: 1. The puzzle
panels.caption: Each computer has graphs with local quirks and shared cluster traits mixed together.

panels.title: 2. The blind approach
panels.caption: All machines send their full learned patterns. Server averages them, mixing local and cluster traits.

panels.title: 3. The paper's move
panels.caption: On each machine, separate the personalized local patterns from the cluster patterns before uploading.

panels.title: 4. Smart aggregation
panels.caption: Server receives only cluster patterns and aggregates them cleanly without local noise.

panels.title: 5. The payoff
panels.caption: Each machine gets personalized feedback for its local graphs plus accurate shared clustering.

steps.text: Analyze your local graphs and split each into a personalized part (your quirks) and a cluster part (the shared pattern).
Keep the personalized parts local for privacy. Compress the cluster patterns into a compact digest (a summary) and send to the server.
The server collects digests from all machines without the noise of local quirks muddying the picture.
The server measures how each machine's cluster pattern relates to every cluster it could belong to.
The server sends back a personalized guidance signal for each machine, telling it which cluster prototypes to follow.

paras: Instead of sending your entire learned pattern to the server, you send only the cluster-defining part (a pattern digest). The personalized local quirks stay private on your machine and are never uploaded.
object.object: What gets sent to the server

hidden.name: cluster-oriented invariant patterns
paras: A cluster-oriented pattern is the part of your learned model that would apply to any graph in your cluster — the shared signature. It is invariant (stays the same across your graphs in that cluster), not something unique to one graph's privacy. The paper measures this by learning a graph neural network (a model that reads the structure of graphs) and factoring it into two pieces: the invariant cluster-defining part, and the variant personalized part that differs from graph to graph.

The method estimates the cluster pattern by training on each machine using a loss function (error measure) that explicitly penalizes mixing the two types: it rewards finding a part that generalizes across graphs in your cluster and punishes using it for local idiosyncrasies. The server then uses these cluster patterns to decide how to update its prototypes (the canonical examples of each cluster).

heat.caption: Darker means more cluster-oriented. Only the highlighted cluster patterns are sent; local parts stay private.

reads.html: Each machine has two parts: a personalized pattern that differs from graph to graph (the variant), and a shared cluster pattern that stays the same across your cluster (the invariant). The server sees only the invariant.

The paper decomposes the learned graph representation into two factors: personalized variant subgraphs and cluster-oriented invariant subgraphs, minimizing a loss that decouples them during client-side training.

mechanism.h2: Why separating patterns fixes the clustering
paras: The core insight: when you send a mixed pattern (local plus cluster together), the server has no way to know which part is which. It treats them equally, so local noise gets averaged across all machines, corrupting the cluster prototype. But if you separate them first, you can upload only the cluster part — the part designed to generalize to your entire cluster. The server then mixes only these cluster patterns, which are genuinely comparable across machines.

The second move: the server uses the relation between each machine's cluster pattern and each possible cluster to decide how much weight to give that machine's pattern when updating the cluster prototype. This is adaptive aggregation — machines whose cluster patterns fit cluster 3 get heavier weight when updating cluster 3's prototype, and zero weight for clusters they do not belong to. This prevents a machine from cluster 1 from dragging down the prototype for cluster 5.
The result: local privacy (personalized patterns never leave the machine) plus accurate clustering (the server gets clean cluster patterns to work with and knows how to blend them correctly).

stages.s: Split into local (keep) and cluster pattern (copy)
Upload cluster pattern digest to server
Server measures pattern relation to each cluster
Adaptively blend cluster patterns by relation strength
Personalized feedback sent back to each machine

math.h2: The separation loss and adaptive aggregation
math.words: At each machine, minimize (graph encoding error) plus (penalty for mixing local and cluster parts). At server, update cluster prototype by weighting each machine's pattern by its relation score to that cluster.
math.equation: L_client = MSE(encoding, graph) + lambda * (cross_term for mixing); cluster_prototype_k = sum_i (relation_score_ik * pattern_i) / sum_i relation_score_ik
symbols: the training error at one machine
mean squared error, how far your encoding is from the graph truth
how much to penalize mixing local and cluster parts
how much machine i's cluster pattern matches cluster k
the canonical pattern for cluster k at the server

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Machine A (cluster 1) trains and separates its pattern into local (quirk) + cluster (shared).
Cluster pattern from A scores 0.9 relation to cluster 1, 0.1 to cluster 2.
Machine B (also cluster 1) scores 0.85 to cluster 1, 0.15 to cluster 2.
Server updates cluster 1 prototype by blending A and B: (0.9 * A_pattern + 0.85 * B_pattern) / (0.9 + 0.85).
Each machine receives personalized signal: weights to apply to local graphs for cluster 1.

math.note: The key is that machines only send their cluster part, and the server weights by how well that part aligns with each cluster, eliminating the averaging of incompatible local patterns.

charts.title: Naive federated average
charts.note: Averaging all patterns together confuses local quirks with cluster traits, lowering all metrics.

charts.title: FGCN-DKS (this paper)
charts.note: Separating local and cluster patterns improves clustering because the server receives only the patterns designed to generalize across your cluster, not local quirks that would mislead aggregation. Privacy stays perfect because local patterns never leave your machine.

items.html: If the machine does not truly separate the two patterns (the loss function is not strong enough), local quirks leak into the cluster digest. The server still mixes incompatible patterns, defeating the whole approach.

If a machine's graphs actually belong to cluster 3, but the local training pulls its cluster pattern toward cluster 5, the adaptive weights will assign it wrongly and feedback will mislead the machine.
Sending cluster pattern digests from thousands of machines to the server and receiving personalized feedback signals doubles communication. If bandwidth is the bottleneck, this method costs more.
When the separation loss is carefully tuned, clusters are truly separable in the feature space, and machines have stable local data, the method cleanly splits privacy and clustering concerns.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Simulate three machines, each with graphs from two clusters mixed in. Machine 1 has ten graphs from cluster A and five from cluster B (real local imbalance). Machine 2 has six A and nine B. Machine 3 has eight A and seven B. Train FGCN-DKS on each machine for five rounds of federated communication. Measure: (1) does the cluster purity at the server improve each round, because the server is now receiving clean cluster patterns instead of mixed local-plus-cluster confusion? (2) do the local graph encodings on each machine stay consistent across rounds, because separation keeps local patterns stable while receiving only cluster guidance that does not contradict them? (3) when you compute the cluster pattern digests, verify that the local variant parts are truly discarded and never sent to the server.
demo.metric_eq: cluster_purity = (number of graphs in majority cluster) / (total graphs in assigned cluster); local_stability = correlation of graph embeddings before and after round t; bytes_sent = size of cluster digests + feedback signals (should exclude local variant patterns)
demo.closing: The demo succeeds when purity climbs above 80%, local graph encodings (the learned numerical summaries of each graph) remain stable across communication rounds, and you can confirm that variant patterns are never transmitted.
